name: Nd:YAG / Q-switched laser
lead: A Q-switched Nd:YAG laser is a neodymium-doped yttrium aluminium garnet laser that uses Q-switching, an intracavity shutter-like technique, to release stored energy as very short, high-peak-power pulses lasting tens of nanoseconds.[1] In dermatology it is used mainly to treat pigmented lesions and to remove tattoos, and it is discussed in appearance communities as a treatment for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (PIH), melasma and redness.[1]

Wikipedia describes Nd:YAG as among the most favoured lasers for tattoo removal because of its high peak power, high repetition rate and relatively low cost.[1] Published clinical research on appearance uses consists largely of small trials and case series; published evidence for appearance uses is limited, and several registered trials are small or of unknown status.[2][3]
infobox: Tattoo removal, benign pigmented lesions, melasma (off-label)

paras: Q-switching works by keeping losses in a laser cavity high while the gain medium is pumped, so energy accumulates, then lowering the losses to release it as a single giant pulse. Active versions use an acousto-optic or Pockels-cell switch; passive versions use a saturable absorber.[1] Nd:YAG lasers are a common Q-switched type.[1]

In skin, the short pulses are intended to shatter pigment particles such as tattoo ink, which the body then clears through the lymphatic system. Wikipedia notes that full tattoo removal typically takes 6 to 20 treatments spaced at least a month apart.[1] Hair-removal Nd:YAG systems at 1064 nm are generally long-pulsed rather than Q-switched and are described as suited to darker skin.[4]

Gordon Gould proposed Q-switching in 1958, and Robert Hellwarth and F. J. McClung demonstrated it in a ruby laser at Hughes Research Laboratories in 1961-62.[1] Early clinical papers applied Q-switched Nd:YAG pulses to the eye, for example for pupillary and angle-block conditions, in the 1980s.[5] Dermatologic combinations, such as a quadruple-frequency Q-switched Nd:YAG with sclerotherapy for small leg veins and residual pigmentation, were reported by 1998.[6]

Published studies on skin cover tattoo removal, benign pigmented lesions, melasma, solar lentigines, macular amyloidosis and acne scars in registered trials, mostly small (about 4 to 45 participants) and often single-centre.[7][8][9][10] One registered trial compared picosecond and Q-switched lasers for benign pigmented lesions in 20 participants, and another compared picosecond and nanosecond lasers for tattoo removal in 42.[8][9] A pilot trial combined the laser with platelet-rich plasma for melasma (30 participants).[7] A 1998 case series reported combining sclerotherapy with a quadruple-frequency Q-switched Nd:YAG for telangiectases and residual pigmentation.[6] No specific trial results are summarised here; no large controlled trial of Q-switched Nd:YAG for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation or redness is has been published in the sources reviewed here.

For laser hair removal with Nd:YAG, Wikipedia lists burns, skin discoloration, hypopigmentation, purpura, scabbing and infection as possible effects.[4] Wikipedia's laser resurfacing article notes that laser treatments can cause scarring, hyperpigmentation and herpes outbreaks, though it does not discuss Q-switched devices specifically.[11]

timeline.event: Q-switching demonstrated in a ruby laser by Hellwarth and McClung.[1]

card.summary: Nanosecond-pulse laser used by clinics for tattoos and pigment; evidence for appearance uses is mostly small trials.
card.aka: Q-switched laser, QS Nd:YAG, 1064/532 nm laser
card.note: Burns and pigment changes are reported risks, especially on darker skin.

quick.overview:
A Q-switched Nd:YAG laser emits extremely short, powerful pulses. Clinics use it mainly for tattoo removal and pigmented spots, and it is discussed online for dark marks and redness.

Published evidence for appearance uses consists largely of small trials, many without reported results here.
quick.mechanism: Stored laser energy is released as nanosecond pulses meant to shatter pigment particles, which the body then clears.
quick.risks: Reported effects include burns, discoloration, hypopigmentation, scabbing and infection. It is a clinic device operated by trained practitioners.
